title: THE MAN PAUL HANDED OVER TO SATAN—AND THE TERRIFYING REASON IT MAY HAVE BEEN AN ACT OF LOVE
paragraphs:
THE MAN PAUL HANDED OVER TO SATAN—AND THE TERRIFYING REASON IT MAY HAVE BEEN AN ACT OF LOVE
There is a sentence in your Bible so severe that many Christians would rather rush past it. But buried inside those frightening words is something astonishing: Paul was not trying to destroy a sinner. He wanted a sinner saved.
There are Bible verses we underline because they comfort us.
There are verses we post because they inspire us.
And then there are verses that make us stop.
Read them again.
And quietly wonder...
“Did the Bible really just say that?”
This is one of them.
A scandal had erupted inside the church at Corinth.
Not outside the church.
Inside it.

A man identified with the Christian community was involved in sexual immorality of such a shocking kind that Paul said it was not even commonly tolerated among the surrounding Gentiles: a man “had” his father’s wife.
Yet perhaps the most disturbing part of the chapter is not merely what the man had done.
It is what the church had apparently become willing to tolerate.
Paul writes that instead of mourning, they had become arrogant.
Then comes the sentence that has disturbed readers for centuries.
In the original Greek of 1 Corinthians 5:5:
“παραδοῦναι τὸν τοιοῦτον τῷ Σατανᾷ εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκός, ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ ἐν τῇ ἡμέρᾳ τοῦ κυρίου.”
A careful, fairly literal rendering is:
“To hand such a one over to Satan for the destruction of the flesh, so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord.”
Read the final words again.
Because they change everything.
“So that the spirit might be saved.”
Paul's objective was not revenge.
It was not humiliation for entertainment.
It was not religious cruelty dressed up as holiness.
Something far more sobering was happening.
Paul was willing to let a man experience the terrible consequences of refusing repentance because something infinitely more valuable than the man's temporary comfort was at stake.
His soul.
And suddenly this ancient scandal begins getting uncomfortably close to home.
Because perhaps the most dangerous thing that can happen to you is not that God allows your comfortable life to collapse.
Perhaps the most dangerous thing is being allowed to remain comfortable while sin quietly destroys you.
We have created a Christianity where many people think love means affirmation.
Jesus never taught that.
Biblical love does not celebrate what is killing the person it loves.
A doctor who discovers cancer and says nothing because the diagnosis might upset you is not compassionate.
A father watching his child walk toward traffic does not whisper, “I respect your journey.”
Love intervenes.
Love warns.
Love sometimes wounds before the wound becomes fatal.
And Corinth had forgotten this.
Paul had received a report of sexual immorality in the congregation, and instead of the church grieving over the spiritual destruction taking place, they had apparently become puffed up.
The Greek is striking.
Paul says:
“καὶ ὑμεῖς πεφυσιωμένοι ἐστέ”
“You have become puffed up.”
The verb carries the idea of becoming inflated with pride.
Imagine the tragedy.
A man's spiritual life is collapsing...
sexual sin has invaded the fellowship...
the holiness of Christ's church is being publicly contradicted...
and somehow people are still proud of themselves.
That may be one of the most frightening pictures of spiritual blindness in the New Testament.
Because you can become so sophisticated about grace that you stop grieving over sin.
You can become so afraid of sounding judgmental that you stop warning people headed toward destruction.
You can even use the vocabulary of love to protect the very bondage from which Jesus died to deliver us.
But grace never makes peace with the sin that nailed Christ to the cross.
Grace forgives sinners.
Grace cleanses sinners.
Grace restores sinners.
Grace transforms sinners.
Grace does not look at chains and rename them freedom.
Paul therefore commands the church to remove this persistently immoral man from their fellowship.
And this is where we need to understand the frightening phrase:
“παραδοῦναι...τῷ Σατανᾷ”
“To hand over...to Satan.”
Paul uses remarkably similar language elsewhere.
In 1 Timothy 1:20, speaking of Hymenaeus and Alexander, he writes:
“I handed [them] over to Satan so that they might be disciplined not to blaspheme.”
Notice something easily missed.
Again, the purpose is corrective.
“So that they might be disciplined.”
The Greek verb connected with that purpose, παιδεύω, belongs to the language of training, instruction, correction, or discipline.
Paul's goal was not simply, “Make them suffer.”
It was, in effect:
May discipline teach them what rebellion refused to teach them.
That changes how we should hear 1 Corinthians 5.
The Corinthian offender was to be removed from the protected fellowship of the gathered church and placed outside its recognized communion.
Paul later says plainly:
“Remove the evil person from among yourselves.”
This was church discipline at its most severe.
But even severe discipline had a redemptive horizon.
“...so that the spirit might be saved in the day of the Lord.”
Do not miss the heart beating underneath the severity.
Paul wanted the man back.
Back from deception.
Back from sexual bondage.
Back from rebellion.
Back from spiritual numbness.
Back under the lordship of Jesus Christ.
Back to repentance.
Back to life.
Sometimes grace comes running toward you with open arms.
Sometimes grace stands in your path and refuses to let you keep pretending.
Sometimes grace whispers.
Sometimes grace overturns tables.
Sometimes grace says, “Neither do I condemn you.”
And that same grace says, “Go, and from now on sin no more.”
Because Jesus did not shed His blood merely to make us comfortable while remaining enslaved.
He came to save us from our sins.
This is where the passage becomes personal.
Maybe nobody has removed you from a church.
Maybe nobody knows what you are doing.
Maybe your reputation is intact.
Your family thinks you're okay.
People still call you brother.
Sister.
Pastor.
Leader.
Believer.
You still know when to say “Amen.”
You know the worship songs.
You know the Christian language.
But there is a room inside your life where Jesus has been knocking...
and you keep locking the door.
The affair nobody knows about.
The pornography deleted from your history but not your appetite.
The bitterness you have baptized as discernment.
The secret messages.
The money.
The addiction.
The hatred.
The manipulation.
The relationship you know dishonors Christ.
The pride that refuses correction.
The double life that has become so normal you barely feel conviction anymore.
And perhaps you have been interpreting God's patience as God's permission.
That is dangerous.
Romans 2 teaches that God's kindness is intended to lead us toward repentance.
His patience is mercy.
But mercy should never become an excuse for rebellion.
There comes a terrifying point when God may allow a person to taste the bitter fruit of what that person insists on choosing.
Not because sin suddenly became stronger than God.
But because consequences can sometimes awaken what comfort allowed to sleep.
Think of the prodigal son.
The father did not travel into the far country every evening to replenish the son's money so that rebellion could remain comfortable.
The son eventually found himself emptied.
Hungry.
Humiliated.
Looking at food meant for pigs.
And somewhere in that wreckage...
“He came to himself.”
Sometimes the pigpen reveals what the party concealed.
Sometimes losing what you worshipped reveals what you should have worshipped all along.
Sometimes the collapse you begged God to prevent becomes the place where you finally hear Him.
That does not mean every tragedy is God's punishment for a specific sin. Scripture does not permit us to make that reckless conclusion.
It does mean God loves His children too deeply to treat rebellion as harmless.
Hebrews tells us that the Lord disciplines those He loves.
Discipline and rejection are not identical.
Sometimes discipline is evidence that God refuses to abandon His children to destruction.
And this is where Paul's phrase becomes even more difficult:
“εἰς ὄλεθρον τῆς σαρκός”
“For the destruction of the flesh.”
What exactly does that mean?
Christians should resist pretending the interpretive question is simpler than it is.

The Greek word σάρξ—sarx, “flesh”—can refer to the physical body, but Paul can also use “flesh” in ways connected to fallen human existence and sinful inclination. Because of this, interpreters have understood Paul's language differently. Some see possible physical suffering or even death; others understand the destruction as the breaking of sinful fleshly rebellion through severe discipline.
We should not claim more certainty than Scripture gives us.
But Paul's stated purpose is unmistakable:
“ἵνα τὸ πνεῦμα σωθῇ”
“So that the spirit might be saved.”
Salvation—not annihilation—is where Paul's sentence is pointing.
And that means church discipline, properly practiced, is not supposed to be ecclesiastical revenge.
It is not permission for pastors to become tyrants.
It is not authorization for Christians to publicly humiliate people they dislike.
It is not spiritual abuse.
Biblical discipline should mourn.
Paul asked why the Corinthians had not mourned.
That one word exposes so much counterfeit holiness.
Because when another believer falls, the Christian response should never secretly enjoy the scandal.
We should not feast on someone's collapse.
We should not turn another person's worst moment into entertainment.
We should not become excited because somebody else's sin makes our righteousness look brighter.
We mourn.
Because this is a human being.
A soul.
Someone Christ calls to repentance.
Someone who could have been you.
Someone who, apart from grace, is you.
There is no room at the foot of the cross for proud executioners.
Only sinners who know where mercy found them.
And then something extraordinary appears later in Paul's correspondence with Corinth.
In 2 Corinthians 2, Paul speaks about an offender who had received punishment from the majority. Now Paul says something almost shocking after the severity we have just encountered.
The punishment is enough.
Forgive him.
Comfort him.
Reaffirm your love for him.
Why?
Because the man could become overwhelmed by excessive sorrow.
Stop there.
Christian discipline had reached its redemptive purpose, and Paul refused to allow discipline to become permanent condemnation.
This is crucial.

Some interpreters have connected the offender of 2 Corinthians 2 with the sexually immoral man of 1 Corinthians 5. That identification is possible and has a long history, but the text does not explicitly tell us they are the same man, so we should not present the connection as proven fact.
But whether or not these passages describe the same individual, the Gospel pattern could not be clearer.
Sin must be confronted.
Repentance must matter.
And the repentant must not be crushed beneath endless shame.
Paul tells them to forgive.
Comfort.
Reaffirm love.
And then he gives a reason that should make every unforgiving church tremble.
So that Satan does not outwit us.
Think about the irony.
In 1 Corinthians 5, a man is handed over to Satan with salvation as the stated goal.
In 2 Corinthians 2, the church is warned that Satan can gain an advantage when forgiveness and restoration are withheld.
The enemy does not care which ditch destroys you.
He will whisper while you sin:
“It doesn't matter.”
Then when conviction finally breaks you, he changes his sermon:
“You can never come back.”
Before repentance, Satan minimizes sin.
After repentance, he maximizes shame.
Before the fall:
“God will forgive you.”
After the fall:
“God could never forgive you.”
Same liar.
Different sentence.
And somebody reading this has been living under the second sentence for years.
You repented.
But you still hate yourself.
You confessed.
But you still replay it.
You believe Jesus forgives other people.
You preach grace to everybody except the person staring back from your mirror.
Your scandal happened five years ago.
Ten years ago.
Twenty.
But every time you try to worship, your memory drags the old evidence into the courtroom.
“Remember what you did?”
Yes.
You remember.
But perhaps hell is hoping you forget something infinitely greater.
What Jesus did.
The Gospel is not the announcement that your sin wasn't serious.
The cross proves it was deadly serious.
The Gospel is the announcement that Jesus Christ took sin so seriously that He bore its judgment Himself for everyone who turns to Him in repentant faith.
Your forgiveness was not purchased cheaply.
It was purchased with blood.
Jesus was betrayed.
Mocked.
Beaten.
Crucified.
The sinless Son of God carried the judgment sinners deserved.
And He rose from the grave.
That means Christianity does not offer sinners denial.
It offers something infinitely better.
A Savior.
You do not need to rename your sin.
You can confess it.
You do not need to defend your darkness.
You can bring it into the light.
You do not need to pretend the scandal never happened.
You can bring the scandal to the cross.
Because Jesus specializes in stories everybody else thinks are already over.
Peter denied Him.
Christ restored him.
Paul persecuted Christians.
Christ turned him into an apostle.
The thief reached the end of his ruined life with nothing left to offer Jesus but faith...
and discovered that grace can reach a dying criminal on a cross.
This is the Gospel.
Not good people earning God's approval.
Guilty people receiving mercy through Jesus Christ and being transformed by the Holy Spirit.
From scandal...
to grace.
Because Jesus rewrites everything.
But please hear this carefully.
Grace does not mean everybody automatically receives salvation regardless of repentance and faith.
Jesus calls us to repent and believe the Gospel.
The cross is not God's permission slip for continuing comfortably in rebellion.
The cross is God's invitation to die to the old life and belong to Christ.
Maybe this article did not reach you because you needed an interesting explanation of an uncomfortable Bible verse.
Maybe you needed a mirror.
What are you protecting that Jesus is asking you to surrender?
What sin have you been calling “a struggle” when deep inside you know you have stopped fighting it?
What relationship are you unwilling to place beneath Christ's authority?
What secret would terrify you if it appeared on a screen in front of everybody you love?
You do not have to tell the internet every detail.
But you need to stop lying to God.
And maybe, finally...
to yourself.
Come home.
Not after you fix yourself.
Not when you feel worthy.
Not when the consequences disappear.
Come to Jesus now.
Confess.
Repent.
Believe.
Ask for help.
Bring another mature, trustworthy believer into the battle where appropriate.
Cut off what keeps pulling you backward.
Stop negotiating with the thing Christ died to free you from.
And when you fall, do not run away from the Savior.
Run toward Him.
“If we confess our sins, he is faithful and just to forgive us our sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.”
That is 1 John 1:9.
Not because confession purchases forgiveness.
Christ purchased forgiveness.
Confession stops pretending we do not need it.
And perhaps the church needs repentance too.
Because some churches have confused tolerance with grace.
Others have confused cruelty with holiness.
Jesus gives us permission for neither.
Truth without love becomes a weapon.
“Love” without truth becomes permission to die quietly.
But in Jesus Christ we encounter grace and truth.
The church should be one of the hardest places in the world to comfortably cherish unrepentant sin...
and one of the safest places in the world for a broken sinner genuinely seeking Christ to confess, repent, heal, and come home.
Imagine that church.
A church where holiness matters.
Where nobody celebrates sin.
Where leaders are accountable too.
Where discipline is never weaponized to protect powerful people.
Where repentance is real.
Where forgiveness is real.
Where broken people are not discarded.

Where restoration does not necessarily erase every earthly consequence or automatically restore every former position, but where repentant people are still treated as human beings for whom Christ's mercy is not exhausted.
That is the difference between biblical restoration and cheap grace.
Forgiveness does not mean pretending nothing happened.
Restoration does not always mean returning someone immediately—or ever—to the same position of authority.
Trust may require time.
Victims must not be pressured into unsafe reconciliation.
Crimes should not be concealed beneath religious language.
Church discipline must never become a shield for abuse.
But neither should a genuinely repentant believer be sentenced by Christians to lifelong spiritual exile after Christ has extended mercy.
We are not the Savior.
Jesus is.
Maybe now you understand why this disturbing chapter belongs inside the Gospel story.
The man Paul handed over to Satan was not being treated as though his soul were worthless.
The severity existed precisely because his soul mattered.
Sin mattered.
The church mattered.
The holiness of Christ mattered.
Eternity mattered.
And salvation mattered.
Which leaves us with a question far more frightening than:
“Why would Paul hand someone over to Satan?”
The deeper question may be:
What if God loves us enough to destroy the comfortable lies keeping us from repentance?
What if the closed door saved you?
What if being exposed saved you?
What if losing the relationship woke you up?
What if the consequence you hated finally made you confront the bondage you loved?
What if the night you thought God had abandoned you became the night you finally stopped running from Him?
We should never romanticize suffering or assume every painful event is divine discipline.
But Scripture gives us something better than a promise of uninterrupted comfort.
It gives us a God who works even through discipline for the good of His children.
A Father who loves.
A Savior who bleeds.
A Spirit who convicts.
A Gospel that tells the truth about our sin without surrendering us to despair.
Not because typing words saves you.
Only Jesus saves.
But sometimes bringing the struggle into the light is the first crack in a wall we have spent years building.

And if Christ has already brought you through your own season of rebellion, discipline, repentance, or restoration, tell someone what His grace has done. Your testimony may become the reason another ashamed believer realizes that coming home is still possible.
Not because every paragraph is comfortable.
Send it privately to the believer who thinks he has gone too far.
Send it to the sister who cannot forgive herself.
Send it to the person who needs somebody to love them enough to tell the truth.
Stay close to daily Scripture, biblical truth, conviction, encouragement, healing, discipleship, and spiritual nourishment centered on Christ.

And if this ministry is helping you glorify God, consider supporting the work rather than merely consuming it. We support Christian ministry because we want Gospel-centered work to continue reaching people.
Not to glorify Gospel Warrior.
Not to glorify yourself.
Do it, if you choose to do it, to point another human being toward Jesus.
Someone whose marriage is dying.
Someone hiding an addiction.
Someone convinced God no longer wants them.
Someone comfortable in sin.
Someone drowning in shame after repentance.
Someone who will never tell you how close they were to giving up.
You may never know which sentence reaches them.
You may never know which share interrupts someone's darkness.
You may never know which testimony sends a prodigal walking home.
But you can refuse to hide the light you have received.
And before you leave this article, remember the man in Corinth.
Remember the scandal.
Remember the terrifying sentence.
Remember its purpose.
“So that the spirit might be saved.”
The Gospel is severe about sin because Calvary reveals how deadly sin really is.
But Calvary also reveals something else.
There is mercy for sinners.
Real sinners.
Exposed sinners.
Disgraced sinners.
Church sinners.
Secret sinners.
People whose stories contain chapters they wish they could burn.
Jesus Christ did not come for imaginary people with sanitized histories.
He came to save sinners.
So repent.
Come into the light.
Receive His grace.
And let Him begin writing what shame told you could never be written.
Because sometimes the chapter that feels like the end of your story is only the place where grace finally takes the pen.
